name: Yoruba

population.definition: Estimate of 'the total number of Yoruba people in West Africa' (people, not strictly speakers); no year given in the extract; same page cautions Nigerian census figures are often inaccurate. Nigeria's 2006 census asked no ethnicity question (per a search summary only, not read on a source page).

source.title: Geography and Society (ch. 1, The Yoruba from Prehistory to the Present)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: the total number of Yoruba people in West Africa is estimated to be about 40 million

facts.claim: Yoruba-speaking communities live mostly in six south-west Nigerian states (Lagos among them), with groups in Benin (formerly Dahomey) and Togo, and a presence in Cuba, Brazil, Haiti and Peru.

source.title: Geography and Society (ch. 1, The Yoruba from Prehistory to the Present)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: Outside Africa, Yoruba are present in Cuba, Brazil, Haiti, Peru.

facts.claim: The book describes the Yoruba as one of the largest ethnic groups in West Africa with major populations in Nigeria, Benin and Togo.

source.title: The Yoruba from Prehistory to the Present (book page)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: one of the largest ethnic groups in West Africa

facts.claim: Before the 19th century there was no general name for the Yoruba as a whole; the name was first applied to the Oyo (by Fulani or Hausa speakers, per the chapter) and the collective identity dates to the 19th century, shaped by missionaries and the early Yoruba elite.

source.title: Geography and Society (ch. 1)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: originally given to the Oyo people by the Fulani or the Hausa

facts.claim: Origin legend of Oduduwa establishes Ile-Ife as the cradle of the Yoruba; the chapter dates the start of Yoruba history studies to Oduduwa's arrival story and to Crowther and Johnson onwards.

source.title: Geography and Society (ch. 1)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: establishes Ile-Ife as the cradle of the Yoruba

facts.claim: Ife was established around the 11th century and known for its artisans; its heads depict the ooni, rulers of Yoruba kingdoms.

source.title: Nigerian Treasures: Ife heads
source.author: Eric García
source.quote: Established around the 11th century, Ife was well known for the skill of its artisans.

facts.claim: Urbanisation: the chapter describes the Yoruba as highly urbanised, with town unions organised by educated migrants in Lagos and other large towns. (Extract via page summary tool; verify wording before publishing. Ibadan appears only as a dialect area; no readable source on Ibadan/Lagos size.)

timeline.claim: Ife established as a kingdom known for its artisans.

source.title: Nigerian Treasures: Ife heads
source.author: Eric García
source.quote: Established around the 11th century, Ife was well known for the skill of its artisans.

timeline.claim: Dating given for the Ife bronze (copper-alloy) Ooni head and a terracotta male head; the lost Olokun Head is dated to around 1350 by scholars. (Museum pages from the Met and British Museum were unreadable; this is a magazine caption.)

source.title: Nigerian Treasures: Ife heads
source.author: Eric García
source.quote: Scholars believe it most likely dated to around 1350.

timeline.claim: Major Yoruba polities of the period included Owu, Ijesa, Egba and Ijebu, alongside many smaller polities.
Oyo became a dominant, expansionist polity and, in the 17th century, the main political actor in Yorubaland.

source.title: The Seventeenth Century: The Age of Empire Building (ch. 5)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: The Oyo Empire was the principal political actor in this period

timeline.claim: Oyo's collapse was followed by internecine Yoruba wars lasting until British intervention near the century's end.

source.title: The Nineteenth Century: The Internecine Wars and Consequences (ch. 8)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: heralded a period of internecine Yoruba wars

timeline.claim: An inter-colonial boundary divided Western Yoruba into two jurisdictions (today's Nigeria/Benin line, per chapter context).

source.title: Colonial Rule, Economy, Education, and Identity (ch. 14)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: divided Western Yoruba into two jurisdictions

timeline.claim: Lugard consolidated the protectorates into the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria (ceremony in Lagos, 1 Jan 1914).

source.title: Lord Lugard Created Nigeria 104 Years Ago
source.author: Jack McCaslin
source.quote: creating the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria

source.title: Nigeria60: Realisation of a 99-year dream
source.author: Emeka Keazor
source.quote: Nigeria had become an independent nation

colonial.claim: Collective Yoruba identity dates to the 19th century, shaped by Christian missionaries and the early Yoruba elite; earlier, people identified by subgroup, settlement or area.

source.title: Geography and Society (ch. 1)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: no general name for the Yoruba as a whole

colonial.claim: Late colonial Yoruba politics cannot be separated from national-level developments and rising ethnic awareness among Nigerians more broadly.

source.title: Politics and Yoruba Identity in the Late Colonial Era (ch. 15)
source.author: Aribidesi Usman and Toyin Falola
source.quote: cannot be separated from what was happening at the national level

colonial.claim: Older city/subgroup identities persisted in dialect and institutions, e.g. Egba (Agbeyin, Gbagura, Oke-Ona) and Ijebu (four provinces) with Osugbo and Ogboni societies in judicial roles.

myth.claim: That the Ife heads could not have been made by Africans (Frobenius's 1910 theory attributing the Olokun Head to survivors of Atlantis).
myth.truth: The article calls Frobenius's theories racist and says Ife was known for its artisans and the heads depict ooni, rulers of Yoruba kingdoms.
